newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU ministers agree climate-change cuts target.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU ministers agree climate-change cuts target.

text.p: EU environment ministers opened the bidding on Monday in the search for a year-end international deal to cut industrialised countries' emissions of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels.

In agreeing to cut the bloc's emissions of greenhouse gases by 15 percent of 1990 levels by 2010, albeit without a full deal on which country cuts what, the 15-country bloc laid down a marker for international climate change talks scheduled for Kyoto, Japan in December.
Greenhouse gases trap heat close to the earth's surface and are blamed for what scientists fear will be a long-term warming of the global climate.

"We are very happy with the agreement," an Austrian source, who asked not to be named, told reporters, adding that Vienna had been happy to stick with its commitment to cut emissions by one quarter of 1990 levels by the year 2010.

Ministers agreed on how to share out individual cuts between countries for only 10 percentage points of the 15 percent pledged, an indication of the difficulties the European Union still faces with its announced target.
Dutch Environment Minister Margreet de Boer told reporters late on Sunday that the 15 percent figure was a firm commitment.
"We go to Kyoto with 15 percent and if that's agreed then we will negotiate about how to share out the remaining five percent within the EU," she said.
Plans ahead of the meeting targeted the major greenhouse gas, carbon dioxide (CO2) from burning fossil fuels like coal and oil, to make up 12 percentage points of the EU's proposed 15 percent cut.

The Dutch, as holders of the EU presidency, unusually scheduled the meeting on a Sunday in anticipation of two-day, formal ministerial talks on Monday and international talks by climate negotiators starting on Monday in Bonn.
In reaching a deal, ministers rejigged a previous Dutch proposal, softening the demands on most countries in striking agreement on the overall figure, Dutch diplomats said.
Germany and Britain, two of the EU's major fossil-fuel users, saw their allotted targets cut from 30 percent to 25 per cent and from 20 percent to 10 percent respectively.

The target for France, with a majority of its electricity coming from non-CO2-emitting nuclear power, was cut to zero from the originally suggested five percent reduction while Italy's went from the 10 percent cut proposed to seven percent.

Other countries seeing their targets softened included Ireland, to be allowed a 15 percent emissions increase instead of the suggested five percent rise, Finland, granted an emissions freeze in place of a 10 percent cut and Greece, with a 30 percent increase in place of five percent.
Portugal's allowed emissions figure went up 15 percentage points to 40 percent, Spain's rose two percentage points to 17 percent while Luxembourg's 40 percent cut became 30 percent.
Belgium and the Dutch retained their 10 percent cuts while Austria and Denmark kept their 25 percent cuts and Sweden its five percent rise.

While EU environment ministers now appear to have firmed their line on emissions cuts, EU ministers for transport, energy and, most important of all economy and finance, will all want their say on the detail during the coming months.
